# Target `/workspace/dataset/test14_executable --a --b ` is a PyInstaller build of this Python script: doc1 = f"## Section 1\n{args.a}" doc2 = f"## Section 2\n{args.b}" html1 = markdown.markdown(doc1) html2 = markdown.markdown(doc2) toc_md = "# Table of Contents\n1. Section 1\n2. Section 2" toc_html = markdown.markdown(toc_md, extensions=['toc']) final_doc = f"{toc_html}\n\n{html1}\n\n{html2}" final_html = markdown.markdown(final_doc) print(html1); print(html2); print(toc_html); print(final_html) It bundles Python-Markdown **3.10.2** (no extensions except `toc` on the fixed toc_md). NO fenced_code, NO tables, NO nl2br, NO attr_list, NO smarty. # Goal We are reimplementing `markdown.markdown()` from scratch in pure JavaScript (no deps, no regex-hacks — a real character-scanning parser producing an element tree, exactly mirroring Python-Markdown's architecture: preprocessors -> block parser -> tree processors (inline) -> serializer -> postprocessors). Your job is to produce an EXACT, evidence-backed behavioral specification for your assigned area, precise enough that an implementer who has never seen Python-Markdown's source can reproduce byte-identical output. # How to probe (IMPORTANT) Use bash. To render an isolated document D (so the `## Section 1` prefix does not interfere), pass a leading newline so the doc becomes "## Section 1\n\nD": /workspace/dataset/test14_executable --a $'\n\nD_line1\nD_line2' --b $'\n\nOTHER' The FIRST printed block (up to the line `

Section 2

`) is markdown("## Section 1\n" + a); the second (up to `

`) is markdown("## Section 2\n" + b). Two independent probes per invocation. Write a helper script to reduce noise, e.g. create /tmp//p.sh: #!/bin/bash # usage: p.sh 'markdown text' -> prints only html1 minus the leading

Section 1

out=$(/workspace/dataset/test14_executable --a "$(printf '\n\n%s' "$1")" --b 'z') printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n '2,/^

Section 2<\/h2>$/p' | sed '$d' | cat -A | sed 's/\$$//' Use `cat -A` or `od -c` when trailing whitespace / exact newlines matter — trailing spaces and the presence/absence of a final newline are load-bearing for us. Beware: bash `$(...)` strips trailing newlines, so when trailing-newline behavior matters, write the markdown to a file and use `--a "$(cat file)"`-free approaches like python-free `xargs`? No — instead use: `/workspace/dataset/test14_executable --a "$(printf 'x\n\n')" ...` (printf inside the arg preserves them since it is one argv string). Prefer building args with `printf` into a bash variable using `read -r -d ''` or a heredoc-free literal `$'...'` string, which preserves trailing newlines exactly. Do 40-120 probes. Be systematic: for each rule, find the boundary (what makes it stop applying). # Output Return a JSON object per the schema. Rules must be mechanical and implementable ("if the line, after stripping up to 3 leading spaces, begins with 1-6 '#' followed by ..."). Every rule needs at least one verified input/output pair copied VERBATIM from a real run. Flag anything you could not determine. ---- AREA: inline code spans, backslash escapes, and entity/ampersand handling. - Code spans: single, double, triple, quadruple backticks; unmatched/odd counts; backticks inside; leading/trailing spaces inside a span (stripped?); spans containing newlines (multi-line spans — CRITICAL, see the fenced-code-block case where \`\`\`python\n...\n\`\`\` becomes one `` span); empty span \`\`; span containing `<`, `&`, `>`, `"`, `'` (exact escaping); span containing `\\` and markdown chars; a span spanning a blank line (does it?); interaction with a code span at the very start/end of a paragraph. - Backslash escapes: which characters are escapable (`\\ \` \* \_ \{ \} \[ \] \( \) \# \+ \- \. \! \< \> \| \: \" \' \& \~ \^ \= \, \/ \; \? \@ \$ \% \a \1 \newline \space)? What does a backslash before a non-escapable char produce? Backslash at end of line / end of document. Backslash inside code spans. Double backslash. - Ampersands and entities: bare `&`, `&`, `A`, `A`, ` `, `¬arealentity;`, `&` (no semicolon), `&#`, `& amp;`, `&&`, `&` in a URL, `&` in a code span, `<` and `>` bare, `"` and `'` bare in text vs in attributes. Give the exact escaping table.

attachment.content:
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

input.area: inline code spans, backslash escapes, and entity/ampersand handling

rules.rule:
PRE-STAGE (whitespace normalization, applies to everything below): before any parsing, the source has U+0002 (STX) and U+0003 (ETX) characters deleted, "
" and lone "" replaced by "
", then "

" appended to the end, then tabs expanded to 4-column tab stops, then lines consisting only of spaces emptied. The STX/ETX deletion matters because those two characters are the internal placeholder delimiters.

ENTITY PRE-STAGE (numeric character references are normalized by the HTML-extraction preprocessor, i.e. BEFORE block parsing and BEFORE inline parsing, so it also rewrites text inside code spans and code blocks). Scan the whole normalized document left to right. When an '&' is found: (A) if the next char is '#', try to match, anchored at the '&', the regex `&#(?:[0-9]+|[xX][0-9a-fA-F]+)[^0-9a-fA-F]` (note: greedy digit run, and one MANDATORY trailing character that is NOT a hex digit [0-9a-fA-F]; standard regex backtracking applies). If it matches with total length L, let name = source[i+2 .. i+L-2] (the match minus the leading '&#' and minus its final terminator char); emit the text `&` + `#` + name + `;`; then set k = i+L, and if source[k-1] != ';' set k = k-1; continue scanning at k. If it does NOT match, emit the two literal characters `&#` and continue scanning at i+2. (B) if the next char is not '#', try to match `&([a-zA-Z][-.a-zA-Z0-9]*);` anchored at the '&'; if it matches, emit the matched text verbatim (identity — no observable change) and continue after it; otherwise emit a literal `&` and continue at i+1. Nothing is ever dropped and parsing never aborts.

The entity pre-stage rewrite is observable inside code spans and indented code blocks (proving it happens before block/inline parsing), but NOT inside raw HTML tags (whose text is consumed wholesale by the HTML extractor).

The entity pre-stage never disables later parsing: an unresolvable '&' (e.g. `&nbsp` with no semicolon, or `&#x;`) does not prevent subsequent inline HTML, block-level HTML, or HTML comments from being recognized.

SERIALIZER TEXT ESCAPING (applies to every text/tail string in the element tree, in this order): (1) replace each '&' that is NOT immediately followed by a valid entity reference body with `&` — 'valid' means the regex `&(?:\#[0-9]+|\#[xX][0-9a-fA-F]+|[a-zA-Z0-9]+);` matches starting at that '&'; (2) replace '<' with `<`; (3) replace '>' with `>`. Double quote and single quote are NEVER escaped in text.

SERIALIZER ATTRIBUTE ESCAPING (applies to every attribute value, in this order): (1) same conditional '&' rule as text (escape '&' to `&` only when it does not start a valid entity reference per `&(?:\#[0-9]+|\#[xX][0-9a-fA-F]+|[a-zA-Z0-9]+);`); (2) '<' -> `<`; (3) '>' -> `>`; (4) '"' -> `"`. Single quote is NOT escaped.

Text placed in an 'atomic' (no-further-inline-processing) node, such as autolink link text, is subject only to the serializer's conditional text escaping — a literal `&` there stays `&` (NOT `&amp;`), while a bare `&` becomes `&`.
Text inside stashed raw HTML (block-level HTML, raw tags, comments) bypasses ALL escaping and is emitted byte-for-byte.

INLINE PATTERN PRIORITY (highest first, all relevant to this area): backtick/code-span (190) > backslash-escape (180) > reference (170) > link (160) > image_link (150) > image_reference (140) > short_reference (130) > short_image_ref (125) > autolink (120) > automail (110) > linebreak (100) > raw-inline-html (90) > entity (80) > not_strong (70) > em_strong (60/50). Each pattern is applied repeatedly (one match at a time) over the whole buffer until it no longer matches, before the next-lower pattern is tried. Consequence: code spans are found before escapes, links, and raw inline HTML.

CODE SPAN MATCHING ALGORITHM. Over the current inline buffer, for i = 0,1,2,... try in order: (ALT-1) if (i == 0 or buf[i-1] != '\\') and buf[i] == '\\': let B = length of the run of consecutive backslashes starting at i; if B is even and buf[i+B] == '`', then this is a match that consumes exactly those B backslashes and produces B/2 literal backslash characters (protected from further processing); restart the scan at index 0. (ALT-2) if (i == 0 or buf[i-1] != '\\') and buf[i] == '`': let N = length of the backtick run starting at i; for n = N down to 1: for j = i+n+1 up to len(buf)-n (i.e. earliest j first, content length >= 1): if buf[j..j+n-1] == n backticks AND buf[j-1] != '`' AND (j+n == len(buf) or buf[j+n] != '`') then MATCH — consumed region is buf[i..j+n-1], raw content is buf[i+n..j-1]; produce a <code> element; restart the scan at index 0. If neither alternative matches, advance i by 1. The newline character IS matchable by the content, so code spans may span multiple lines of the same block.

A run of two or more backticks with nothing between them, or with only whitespace between them, still forms a span; if the stripped content is empty the result is ``. A single lone pair of backticks with nothing at all between them (``) is NOT a span because the content must be at least one character.

CODE SPAN CONTENT PROCESSING: raw content is (1) stripped of leading and trailing whitespace using Python `str.strip()` semantics (chars where str.isspace() is true: ' ', '\t', '\n', '\r', '\x0b', '\x0c', '\x1c'-'\x1f', '\x85', '\xa0' NBSP, U+1680, U+2000-U+200A, U+2028, U+2029, U+202F, U+205F, U+3000 — but NOT U+200B ZWSP), then (2) escaped UNCONDITIONALLY: '&' -> `&`, then '<' -> `<`, then '>' -> `>` (quotes and backslashes untouched), then (3) marked atomic so no other inline pattern (escape, link, emphasis, entity, linebreak, raw HTML) applies. Interior whitespace including newlines and "two spaces + newline" is preserved exactly.

Multi-line code spans work within a single block, so a ```` ```python ... ``` ```` fenced-code-looking construct (with no fenced_code extension) becomes ONE <code> span containing `python\n...` — but a code span can NEVER cross a block boundary produced by the block parser (blank line, ATX heading line, setext underline / thematic break line, blockquote '>' line). The block parser runs BEFORE inline processing.

A code span opener is suppressed when the character immediately before the first backtick is a single backslash (odd-length backslash run). With an EVEN-length backslash run immediately before the backticks, ALT-1 fires first: the run is consumed and replaced by half as many literal backslashes, and the span still forms afterwards.
A backslash inside a code span's content does NOT escape the closing backtick — the closing-run search ignores backslashes entirely.

BACKSLASH ESCAPE PATTERN: match `\` followed by any single character (INCLUDING a newline). The exactly-16 escapable characters are: \ ` * _ { } [ ] ( ) > # + - . !  (backslash, backtick, asterisk, underscore, open/close brace, open/close bracket, open/close paren, greater-than, hash, plus, hyphen, period, exclamation). If the following character is one of these, the two-character sequence is replaced by that single character, protected from all further inline processing (but still subject to serializer escaping at the end). NOTE: '<' is NOT escapable.

If the character after the backslash is NOT one of the 16 escapable characters, BOTH characters are left in the text verbatim (the backslash is kept), and the escape scanner resumes AFTER both characters (so that second character can never be re-used as the start of a new escape). Non-escapable includes: < | : " ' & ~ ^ = , / ; ? @ $ % digits letters space tab newline and all non-ASCII.

A backslash immediately followed by a newline is NOT a hard line break: both the backslash and the newline are kept verbatim (a hard break requires two-or-more spaces before the newline, of which exactly the last two are consumed). A backslash at the very end of the document is emitted as a literal backslash.

Backslash sequences are consumed left-to-right in non-overlapping pairs: an even-length run of backslashes yields half as many literal backslashes; with an odd-length run the trailing backslash escapes the character after it (if escapable) or is kept literally with it.

Escaped characters are protected only from INLINE pattern matching, not from serializer escaping: the only escapable character affected is '>', which comes back out as `>` in text and as `>` in attribute values.
Escapes are unescaped inside attribute values too (URLs, titles, alt text), and inside autolink hrefs/text.

When an escaped character ends up inside text that the raw-inline-HTML pattern later matches, the BACKSLASH IS RESTORED (the stashed raw HTML gets `\` + char, not just char). So `<b title="\*x">` is emitted with the backslash intact.

Escapes are inline-level and cannot prevent a block construct by 'escaping the marker'; they work only incidentally because a line starting with `\` no longer starts with the block marker character. Escaping the digit of an ordered list marker does nothing (digits are not escapable), but escaping the '.' does.
Escaping '!' and '[' suppresses image/link syntax; escaping only '!' still leaves the link.

Because code spans are matched before every other inline pattern, a code span at the very start or the very end of a paragraph, or occupying the whole paragraph, behaves identically; and code spans nest inside emphasis/links (as children) but emphasis/links never form inside a code span.

A hard line break (` \n` -> `
\n`) is not produced inside a code span, and trailing spaces at the very end of a paragraph (with no following line) are preserved verbatim in the output.

uncertainties: I could not distinguish, from output alone, whether valid entity references in inline-processed text are (a) extracted into the raw-HTML stash by an inline 'entity' pattern at priority 80 and re-inserted verbatim after serialization, or (b) simply left alone by the serializer's conditional '&' rule. Both models produce identical bytes for every probe I ran (the two regexes are the same). An implementer can safely implement ONLY the serializer's conditional rule (escape '&' unless it starts `&(#[0-9]+|#[xX][0-9a-fA-F]+|[a-zA-Z0-9]+);`) plus the unconditional pre-escape for code-span/code-block content, and get byte-identical output. If some other area depends on entities being opaque to emphasis/word-boundary logic, that needs separate probing.

I verified `A` (uppercase X) is treated as a valid hex charref by BOTH the preprocessor's charref regex and the serializer's attribute/text '&' guard. I inferred the guard regex is `\#[xX][0-9a-fA-F]+` (or an equivalent case-insensitive form). I did not find a probe that could distinguish `[xX]` from a fully case-insensitive regex, but since the only case-variable part is the 'x', this makes no observable difference.

The preprocessor's entity-reference path (`&([a-zA-Z][-.a-zA-Z0-9]*);`) appears observably to be an exact identity transform (emits precisely what it consumed), so I modelled it as a no-op. I could not construct a probe where it changes output. If a future probe shows a difference (e.g. some exotic name), this rule would need revision.

Out of my area but noticed: a link title spanning a newline is emitted with the newline collapsed to a single space (`[a](u "ti\ntle")` -> `title="ti tle"`). I did not determine whether this is whitespace collapsing in the link processor or `\n` handling in the attribute serializer. Whoever specs links should pin this down; it is NOT `
`.
I did not probe escapes/entities inside reference-style link definitions, footnote-like constructs, or the `toc` extension's slugification, since the harness only applies `toc` to a fixed string.
I did not probe surrogate/astral characters or characters above U+FFFF inside code spans or after a backslash; I assume they behave like any other non-escapable, non-whitespace character.

Whether `\x1c`-`\x1f` and `\x85` are actually stripped from code-span edges is inferred from Python `str.strip()` semantics; I directly verified only ' ', '\t' (post tab-expansion), '\n', '\x0b', '\x0c', '\xa0', U+2028 and U+3000 (stripped) and U+200B (not stripped).
